items.title: CENTCOM tells civilians to evacuate Iranian ports along Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: US Military Warns of Possible Strikes on Iranian Civilian ...

items.description:
U.S. Central Command issued an urgent warning on Wednesday telling civilians to "immediately" avoid all port facilities along the Strait of Hormuz where Iranian naval forces are operating, a statement that signals the United States views those sites as potential military targets as the war enters its 12th day.[1][2]

"Iranian dockworkers, administrative personnel, and commercial vessel crews should avoid Iranian naval vessels and military equipment," CENTCOM said in the statement posted to social media. The command said Iran's regime "is using civilian ports along the Strait of Hormuz to conduct military operations that threaten international shipping".[3][4][2][1]

items.title: Rice team turns toxic 'forever chemicals' into battery-grade lithium

featured_image.name: Lithium helps reduce PFAS to reusable fluorine

items.description: Two recent studies are offering cleaner paths to securing lithium — one by repurposing toxic "forever chemicals" to pull lithium from brine, the other by using nothing more than carbon dioxide and water to recycle spent batteries. Together, the advances address twin pressures facing the clean energy transition: growing demand for battery-grade lithium and the environmental toll of obtaining it.

items.title: Arctic sea ice nears record-low winter peak, data shows

featured_image.name: Arctic sea ice hits record low for its usual peak growth period

items.description: Arctic sea ice is on track to reach one of its smallest winter peaks since satellite monitoring began more than four decades ago, according to an AFP analysis of U.S. government data published Wednesday. The finding adds to a cascade of climate indicators showing the rapid transformation of the polar north.

items.title: NASA begins assembling Dragonfly rotorcraft for Titan mission

featured_image.name: NASA's Dragonfly Mission Begins Rotorcraft Integration ...

items.description: NASA's Dragonfly mission has officially entered its integration and testing phase, a milestone that marks the beginning of assembling the nuclear-powered rotorcraft that will one day fly across the surface of Saturn's moon Titan. The work is underway in clean rooms at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Maryland, where engineers are building the car-sized, eight-rotor drone ahead of a planned 2028 launch.[1]

items.title: Israel plans military base in Somaliland to counter Houthis

featured_image.name: Israel to build base in Somaliland to target Houthis, says ...

items.description:
As war with Iran continues, Israel is quietly laying the groundwork for a military and intelligence presence in Somaliland, the breakaway East African territory it recognized in December, with the goal of countering Yemen's Houthi movement from across the Gulf of Aden.

The arrangement would allow Israel to gather intelligence on and conduct operations against the Houthis, according to a Bloomberg report citing two Somaliland officials who requested anonymity. Somaliland's minister of the presidency, Khadar Hussein Abdi, confirmed the trajectory of the partnership in an interview with Bloomberg in Hargeisa. "In terms of security, we will have a strategic relationship and that encompasses a lot of things," Abdi said. "We haven't discussed with them if it becomes a military base, but definitely there will be an analysis at some point."[1][2][3]

items.title: Trump renews threat to cut off trade with Spain over Iran base dispute

featured_image.name: Trump threatens Spain with trade war after it refuses to ...

items.description: President Donald Trump on Wednesday renewed his threat to cut off trade with Spain, telling reporters "we may cut off trade" with the country over its continued refusal to allow U.S. forces to use jointly operated military bases for strikes connected to the conflict with Iran. The fresh warning came as Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez dismissed concerns about U.S. economic reprisals, saying in an interview published late Tuesday that he was "not worried" about possible retaliation.[1][2]

items.title: Synopsys debuts AI chip design tools at Converge 2026

featured_image.name: Synopsys to buy Ansys in a push into AI, chip design ...

items.description: Synopsys on Tuesday launched a suite of new AI-powered chip design and simulation tools at its inaugural Converge 2026 conference in Santa Clara, California, marking the first major product deliveries since the company completed its $35 billion acquisition of Ansys last year.[1]

items.title: Oil prices climb again as nations plan historic reserve release

featured_image.name: Oil Prices Surge as Middle East Conflict Halts Most Strait of Hormuz  Traffic | The New York Sun

items.description: Oil prices resumed their climb on Wednesday, rising more than 3% even as governments signaled plans to release emergency reserves, extending a period of energy-driven turbulence across global financial markets that has pushed up U.S. gasoline prices and rattled bond markets from New Delhi to Frankfurt.

items.title: Trump says 'practically nothing left' to target in Iran

featured_image.name: Trump delivers Iran messaging through exclusive interview spree

items.description:
President Donald Trump declared on Wednesday that American forces have nearly exhausted viable military targets in Iran, telling Axios in a five-minute phone interview that the war will end "soon" because there is "practically nothing left to target" in the country. "Little this and that… Any time I want it to end, it will end," Trump said.[1][2][3]

The remarks came as the joint U.S.-Israeli campaign, dubbed Operation Epic Fury, entered its 12th day. U.S. Central Command reported earlier this week that American forces have struck more than 5,000 targets and damaged or destroyed over 50 Iranian ships since operations began on February 28. Trump also warned Tehran he would retaliate "twenty times harder" should Iran attempt to block oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.[2][4][5]

items.title: IRGC claims strikes on ships in Strait of Hormuz, demands transit approval

featured_image.name: Cargo ship struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz: UK

items.description: Three commercial vessels were struck by unknown projectiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported, in a sharp escalation of attacks on shipping through the world's most critical oil chokepoint. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps appeared to claim responsibility for at least some of the strikes, with IRGC Navy Commander Alireza Tangsiri warning that "any vessel intending to pass must obtain permission from Iran".[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Three commercial ships hit by projectiles in Strait of Hormuz attacks

featured_image.name: Cargo ship catches fire in Strait of Hormuz after three ...

items.description: At least three commercial vessels were struck by unknown projectiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, in the most serious escalation of maritime attacks in the waterway since the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict began nearly two weeks ago.

items.title: Rheinmetall forecasts up to 45% sales growth as Middle East conflict drives demand

featured_image.name: Rheinmetall sees profit jump as Europe prepares for military ...

items.description:
German defense giant Rheinmetall reported record sales and profits for 2025 on Wednesday, forecasting even steeper growth this year as the war in the Middle East opens new business prospects for Europe's largest arms manufacturer.

"Over the weekend the phones did not stop ringing. People want our systems," CEO Armin Papperger told reporters, referring to the company's air defense products. "Well over 100 drones were shot down in the Middle East over the weekend alone with our systems," he added, without naming the countries involved.[1]

items.title: 'Chirp' in distant supernova confirms magnetar engine theory

featured_image.name: Where did this extremely magnetic, dense and dead star come from?  Scientists aren't quite sure

items.description: A strange "chirp" in the light of a distant exploding star has given astronomers the first direct evidence that magnetars — extraordinarily magnetized, rapidly spinning neutron stars — drive the brilliance of superluminous supernovas, resolving a debate that has persisted for more than a decade. The findings, published March 10 in the journal Nature, also mark the first time general relativity has been needed to describe the inner mechanics of a supernova.[1][2]

items.title: Berkeley Lab unveils AI-quantum tool for mapping protein structures

featured_image.name: Why 'quantum proteins' could be the next big thing in biology

items.description: Researchers at the Department of Energy's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and an international team have unveiled a new computing program that combines artificial intelligence with quantum-mechanical calculations to map protein structures faster and more accurately than existing methods. The tool, called AQuaRef — short for AI-enabled Quantum Refinement — was described in a study published in Nature Communications and announced by Berkeley Lab on March 10.[1][2]

items.title: Iran declares U.S., Israeli, allied ships 'legitimate targets' in Hormuz

featured_image.name: The Strait of Hormuz crisis explained: What it means for global shipping

items.description:
Iran's military warned on Wednesday that any vessel belonging to the United States, Israel, or their allies passing through the Strait of Hormuz will be targeted, escalating a maritime crisis that has effectively shut down one of the world's most vital energy corridors.

"Any vessel whose oil cargo or the vessel itself belongs to the United States, the Zionist regime or their hostile allies will be considered legitimate targets," Iran's central operational command, Khatam al-Anbiya, said in a statement carried by state television. The military reiterated that Iran's armed forces "will not allow a single litre of oil to transit" through the strait, adding that the "closure of this strait is the result of conditions imposed by the US and the Zionist regime".[1][2][3]

items.title: IEA proposes record 400M-barrel oil release amid Iran war

featured_image.name: G7 leaders to hold talks to discuss Mideast conflict, oil reserve release

items.description:
French President Emmanuel Macron convened a virtual summit of Group of Seven leaders on Wednesday to address the escalating energy crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, as oil prices whipsawed and the International Energy Agency proposed the largest release of strategic oil reserves in its history.

The leaders' call came after a week of intensifying economic fallout from the conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and has effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply typically transits. France, which holds the rotating G7 presidency, organized the meeting as governments scrambled to contain the damage to global energy markets.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Markets whipsaw as Iran war escalates and CPI data lands

featured_image.name: European markets head for lower open as Iran war continues

items.description:
Global markets swung between gains and losses on Wednesday as investors navigated an intensifying military conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran alongside fresh consumer inflation data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The February Consumer Price Index report, released Wednesday morning, covers a period before the U.S.-Iran war broke out on February 28 and was widely expected to show headline inflation holding steady at 2.4% year over year, with a 0.3% monthly increase, according to FactSet estimates cited by Morningstar. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, was forecast at 0.3% monthly and 2.5% annually. Analysts noted the data would offer limited insight into the economic fallout from the conflict. "This data is from before the recent conflict in the Middle East broke out, so it's not going to give us a whole lot of information on how prices are starting to respond to that," said Josh Jamner, senior investment strategy analyst at ClearBridge, adding that energy price effects would be "a March and April dynamic".[1][2]

items.title: Von der Leyen calls return to Russian energy 'a strategic blunder' amid Iran war

featured_image.name: Speech by President von der Leyen at the European Parliament ...

items.description:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Tuesday that turning back to Russian fossil fuels to ease the energy shock from the Iran war would be "a strategic blunder," even as she acknowledged the conflict has already cost European taxpayers €3 billion in extra energy import costs in just 10 days.[1][2]

Speaking in Strasbourg ahead of the European Council summit scheduled for March 19-20, von der Leyen laid out the scale of the damage: gas prices have risen 50% and oil prices 27% since the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28. "This is the price of our dependency," she said, while insisting that the EU's diversification efforts since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine have left Europe better prepared than before.[3][4][2][1]

items.title: Iran's president's son says new leader is 'safe and sound' amid injury reports

featured_image.name: Slain Ayatollah's son & frontrunner for Supreme Leader is ‘injured in assassination attempt' during air strike

items.description:
Iran's newly appointed Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not appeared publicly, issued a video address, or released a written statement since the Assembly of Experts declared him the country's third supreme leader on March 9, raising mounting questions about his condition amid an ongoing war with the United States and Israel.

Three Iranian officials told The New York Times that Khamenei, 56, sustained injuries including to his legs during the opening day of the U.S.-Israeli military operation on February 28 — the same strikes that killed his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along with dozens of other senior officials and members of the Khamenei family. The officials said the new leader "was alert and sheltering at a highly secure location with limited communication".[1][2][3]

items.title: IEA confirms largest-ever oil reserve release at 400M barrels

featured_image.name: IEA countries to meet later Tuesday on release of oil reserves, but ...

items.description:
The International Energy Agency on Wednesday confirmed it will release 400 million barrels of oil from emergency stockpiles, the largest coordinated intervention in the agency's 52-year history, as governments scramble to contain an energy crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

"The oil market challenges we are facing are unprecedented in scale," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in a statement. "IEA member countries have responded with an emergency collective action of unprecedented size."[1]

The decision, announced at 1300 GMT, came ahead of a virtual meeting of Group of Seven leaders chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron to finalize details of the coordinated response. The release more than doubles the previous record of 182 million barrels that IEA member nations distributed in 2022 following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.[2][3][4][5]
